verses.text: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, there was a certain Levite living on the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim, who took for himself a concubine out of Bethlehem Judah.
His concubine played the prostitute against him, and went away from him to her father’s house to Bethlehem Judah, and was there for four months.

Her husband arose, and went after her, to speak kindly to her, to bring her again, having his servant with him, and a couple of donkeys. She brought him into her father’s house; and when the father of the young lady saw him, he rejoiced to meet him.
His father-in-law, the young lady’s father, kept him there; and he stayed with him three days. So they ate and drank, and stayed there.

On the fourth day, they got up early in the morning, and he rose up to depart. The young lady’s father said to his son-in-law, “Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and afterward you shall go your way.”
So they sat down, ate, and drank, both of them together. Then the young lady’s father said to the man, “Please be pleased to stay all night, and let your heart be merry.”
The man rose up to depart; but his father-in-law urged him, and he stayed there again.
He arose early in the morning on the fifth day to depart; and the young lady’s father said, “Please strengthen your heart and stay until the day declines”; and they both ate.

When the man rose up to depart, he, and his concubine, and his servant, his father-in-law, the young lady’s father, said to him, “Behold, now the day draws toward evening, please stay all night. Behold, the day is ending. Stay here, that your heart may be merry; and tomorrow go on your way early, that you may go home.”
But the man wouldn’t stay that night, but he rose up and departed, and toward Jebus (also called Jerusalem). With him were a couple of saddled donkeys. His concubine also was with him.
When they were by Jebus, the day was far spent; and the servant said to his master, “Please come and let us turn aside into this city of the Jebusites, and stay in it.”
His master said to him, “We won’t turn aside into the city of a foreigner that is not of the children of Israel; but we will pass over to Gibeah.”
He said to his servant, “Come and let us draw near to one of these places; and we will lodge in Gibeah, or in Ramah.”
So they passed on and went their way; and the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
They turned aside there, to go in to stay in Gibeah. He went in, and sat down in the street of the city; for there was no one who took them into his house to stay.
Behold, an old man came from his work out of the field at evening. Now the man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he lived in Gibeah; but the men of the place were Benjamites.
He lifted up his eyes, and saw the wayfaring man in the street of the city; and the old man said, “Where are you going? Where did you come from?”

He said to him, “We are passing from Bethlehem Judah to the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there, and I went to Bethlehem Judah. I am going to Yahweh’s house; and there is no one who has taken me into his house.
Yet there is both straw and feed for our donkeys; and there is bread and wine also for me, and for your servant, and for the young man who is with your servants. There is no lack of anything.”
The old man said, “Peace be to you; how ever let me supply all your needs. Just don’t sleep in the street.”
So he brought him into his house, and gave the donkeys fodder. Then they washed their feet, and ate and drank.

As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain base fellows, surrounded the house, beating at the door; and they spoke to the master of the house, the old man, saying, “Bring out the man who came into your house, that we can have sex with him!”
The man, the master of the house, went out to them, and said to them, “No, my brothers, please don’t act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, don’t do this folly.
Behold, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out now. Humble them, and do with them what seems good to you; but to this man don’t do any such folly.”

But the men wouldn’t listen to him: so the man laid hold of his concubine, and brought her out to them; and they had sex with her, and abused her all night until the morning. When the day began to dawn, they let her go.
Then the woman came in the dawning of the day, and fell down at the door of the man’s house where her lord was, until it was light.

Her lord rose up in the morning, and opened the doors of the house, and went out to go his way; and behold, the woman his concubine had fallen down at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, “Get up, and let us be going!” but no one answered. Then he took her up on the donkey; and the man rose up, and went to his place.
When he had come into his house, he took a knife, and cut up his concubine, and divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the borders of Israel.

It was so, that all who saw it said, “Such a deed has not been done or seen from the day that the children of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt to this day! Consider it, take counsel, and speak.”

footnotes.content: A man loved someone. The text lets us know there was already fracture in this house—he took a concubine, not a wife in the fuller sense. The refrain here, "no king," whispers that without the Lord as our true King, we make our own broken arrangements.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She left him. The text names it plainly—she played the prostitute, then fled to her father's house. Long seasons pass sometimes before a heart can do what it must. Four months is a long silence to sit with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He went after her, servant and donkeys in tow, meaning to speak kindly and bring her home again. How many of us have made this journey—turning back to seek restoration in a broken thing, hoping words might mend what hurt had sundered?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Her father rejoiced to see him. There is warmth here, a father-in-law's genuine welcome, three days of eating and drinking together. Sometimes hospitality speaks louder than words—a home can say 'you are still one of us.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the fourth day, early stirring. The father urges him: 'Strengthen your heart with bread before you go.' There is kindness in the simple offer of food, in the recognition that a journey requires fortifying.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They sat together again. 'Let your heart be merry,' the father says—a simple invitation to linger in fellowship a while longer. We forget sometimes how healing it is to eat with someone, to let the walls come down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The man rose to leave but the father urged him to stay. There is a pattern here of genuine welcome, of someone insisting you are wanted, you belong. This will make what comes next all the more terrible.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fifth day, another departure, another gentle persuasion. 'Wait until evening declines.' The days lengthen, the welcome persists. One might think this is a man being held prisoner—but no, he is simply treasured by this father-in-law.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The father makes his final plea at Gibeah—the very city where horror waits. 'Let your heart be merry' he says again, not knowing the night ahead will shatter that blessing. Sometimes kindness and darkness occupy the same place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But the man rose and went, departing toward Jebus—Jerusalem. He would not stay. We do not know why he refused the father's warmth; the text does not say. Stubbornness, impatience, some private resolve—the reason is silent. That silence matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As dusk fell near Jebus, the servant spoke sense: 'Let us turn in to this city.' Rest offered at the gate of Jerusalem itself—a Jebusite city, yes, but safe. The servant saw what was coming and tried to speak it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The master would not turn in to a foreigner's city. Tribal loyalty spoke louder than wisdom. It is a familiar error—'we do not mix,' 'we do not rest among them.' How many have missed mercy because of the name we give to difference?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Instead they would go to Gibeah, or Ramah—cities of Israel, cities of his own people. The logic seems sound: we will find brothers there, surely they will welcome us. But he was walking toward wolves that wore his own face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sun went down on them as they neared Gibeah, which belonged to Benjamin. Day's end was coming; what they did not know was that darkness of a different kind was settling too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They turned in to Gibeah and sat in the street. Not one person rose to welcome them. The silence of a city unwilling to show mercy—that is the first sign of what a place has become. A home without hospitality is a home without conscience.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An old man came from the field, also from Ephraim, also an outsider in this city of Benjamites. He alone would see the stranger and his family—and move toward them rather than away. One righteous witness often stands alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He lifted his eyes and saw them. Not just saw—saw with the sight that moves the heart to action. 'Where are you going? Where do you come from?' he asks. He is practicing the first act of hospitality: noticing someone's need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Levite answers: 'We are going to Yahweh's house. And there is no one who has taken me in.' This man is a Levite, set apart for service to the Lord—yet he and his household find themselves rejected and homeless in the very city where he seeks shelter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He reassures the old man: 'We are not beggars. We have bread and wine, straw and feed for the donkeys. We lack nothing.' He is offering his own dignity back, saying 'I am not asking for charity, only shelter.' Pride sometimes costs us the mercy we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old man says: 'Peace be to you. Only do not sleep in the street.' There is the old man's wisdom—he knows what the street holds at night in this city. He opens his door to strangers, asking nothing but that they trust him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brought them in, cared for the donkeys, washed their feet, gave them food and drink. This is the texture of true hospitality—each detail an act of welcome, each motion a word to the weary: 'You are safe now. You are home.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As they made merry, the men of the city surrounded the house, pounding at the door, demanding the stranger be brought out for abuse. The warmth inside was suddenly caged by depravity outside. Evil moves in mob form when conscience has fled a place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The old man went out to them and pleaded: 'No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly. This man is under my roof.' He invoked the sacred law of hospitality, the bond that should hold even strangers. But his voice was small against their hunger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He offered his own daughter instead, and the Levite's concubine. The old man grasped at what he thought was lesser evil—a terrible arithmetic of desperation. In such moments, when the mind seeks any escape, it often sells its soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They would not listen. The Levite himself then pushed the concubine out to them. All night, brutalized, abandoned by the man she belonged to. The text marks the moment without decoration: this is what happened. The awfulness is in its plainness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the dawning, she came back to the house and fell at the threshold, her hands on the doorstep. She dragged herself toward shelter, toward the one who cast her out. What broken hope moves a body to seek its abuser's shelter?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He opened the doors in the morning, found her there, and did not speak to her. Did not gather her in his arms. Did not weep. The text does not say he touched her or cried out. Just saw her there and went silent.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He said: 'Get up, let us be going.' No asking if she could walk. No offering of comfort. She did not answer—could not, or would not. So he put her on a donkey and rode toward home as if nothing had changed, as if she had not been unmade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At home, he took a knife and cut her into twelve pieces, sending her throughout the borders of Israel. Whether this was rage or ritual, it was a scream—his way of saying 'Look, see what was done.' The messenger was the body of the dead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in these words of horror: 'Such a deed has not been done.' We like to think we have moved beyond such cruelty—yet the world still dismembers the innocent, and too often we argue about it rather than rise in defense. The Lord sees, and will reckon. As of 2026-10, His mercy toward the broken is still the hope we need.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
